## February 20, 1952 — A Wednesday

You were born on a Wednesday in the middle of winter, and on that exact day in Oslo, Norway, the VI Winter Olympics were in full competition. The Games had opened on February 14th and would run through the 25th, and February 20th fell at the heart of them — speed skating, ski jumping, cross-country racing on the same Norwegian terrain where a German occupation had ended less than seven years earlier. Nations that had been at war were competing on the same courses. It was a pointed, fragile kind of normalcy, and it was happening on your first day alive.

---

**The Metropolitan Museum of Art turned eighty on your birthday.** The Met opened on February 20, 1872 — its first location a brownstone on Fifth Avenue, its collection then modest enough to fit in a carriage. By 1952, it had become one of the great museums of the world, its current building already ancient-seeming, its Egyptian wing drawing crowds. The eightieth anniversary of its opening fell on the day of your birth. You have now outlived that anniversary by forty-six years.

**Fourteen days before you were born, the world acquired a new queen.** King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham on February 6th. His daughter Elizabeth, twenty-five years old, learned she was monarch while on a royal tour in Kenya — she was watching wildlife from a treetop lodge when word reached her. The country she returned to was still wrapped in mourning when you arrived. You were born into the opening days of an Elizabethan era that would last seventy years, until September 2022. The entirety of your adult life unfolded under the same reign.

**The hydrogen bomb had not yet been built.** In February 1952, the Soviet Union had the atomic bomb — tested in 1949, three years earlier — and the United States was months away from testing the first thermonuclear device, which it would do in November 1952 in the Marshall Islands. The weapon that could end civilization as a practical matter did not yet exist when you were born. It existed before your first birthday. The Cold War you grew up inside was not merely ideological. It was a condition of mutual extinction held at bay by the calculation of two governments, and it had been that way since before you were old enough to understand it.

**The Korean War was grinding through its second year with no end in sight.** By February 1952, armistice negotiations had been stalling for seven months at Panmunjom, while the fighting continued along the 38th parallel. Young men were dying for territory neither side could hold decisively, in a war the United States had not declared, for a country most Americans could barely locate. The war ended in July 1953, when you were a year old. You have no memory of a world at war. You were shaped entirely by what came after.

**The jet age was three months away.** On May 2, 1952, the de Havilland Comet entered commercial service — the world's first jet airliner, carrying passengers from London to Johannesburg in roughly half the time a propeller aircraft required. The Comet would later suffer catastrophic structural failures that grounded it, but the age it opened did not close. You were born into a world of propeller planes. You grew up in the jet age, which had arrived before you were old enough to fly anywhere.

---

**The arc of a lifetime.**

You are seventy-four years old in 2026.

Born into a world where polio still emptied swimming pools every summer, three years before Jonas Salk announced a vaccine. Born when roughly a third of American homes had television sets, a fraction that would double within five years. Born in the last months of Harry Truman's presidency, with Dwight Eisenhower about to be elected in November.

You were twelve when Kennedy was assassinated. Seventeen when humans walked on the moon. A young adult through the entire arc of Vietnam. Twenty-four when Nixon resigned. In your thirties for the entirety of the Reagan era. Thirty-seven when the Berlin Wall fell, old enough to understand the full weight of what had seemed permanent giving way in a single night. Forty-nine on September 11, 2001.

The span from your birth to now contains the hydrogen bomb, the polio vaccine, the Civil Rights Act, the moon landing, the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone, and a global pandemic. Each of these was, in its moment, incomprehensible from the vantage point of the one before it.

The Oslo athletes competing on the day of your birth skied and skated in a world without any of it. That world is now as remote as the world of Pompeii. You have lived the entire distance between them.
